newsitem.title: CHINA: China export upturn seen persisting through 1997.
newsitem.headline: China export upturn seen persisting through 1997.

text.p: A government move to revive China's exports by speeding up payment of export tax rebates, coupled with declining domestic demand, have fuelled a swelling trade surplus, newspapers and economists said on Wednesday.

China posted a trade surplus of $10.29 billion for the first four months of this year compared with a deficit of $607 million for the same period of last year, General Administration of Customs figures showed.
Exports in the first four months climbed by 26.9 percent to $50.29 billion compared with the same period last year.
Imports in the same period dipped by 0.5 percent to $40 billion.
The upturn in exports was expected to continue through 1997, said a researcher with the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.
"If exports keep rising up to June, then the upturn is expected to last for the whole year," he said.
The previous slow pace of government payment of export tax rebates to exporters had discouraged many firms from exporting in 1996, giving a lower base rate, he said.
However, the government had taken measures to accelerate payment of export tax rebates to try to revive exports, he said without elaborating.
In addition, slow domestic demand partly caused by the continued relatively tight monetary policy had forced more manufacturers to look to overseas markets for sales, he said.

From January to April, general trade exports rose by 35.2 percent to $21.82 billion from the same year-ago period while exports of processed goods jumped 21.4 percent to $27.3 billion, the figures showed.
General trade imports were down while processed goods imports were rising. No figures were available.
In the first four months, exports of industrial goods reached $43.15 billion, up 27.8 percent, while exports of primary products were $7.15 billion, a rise of 21.5 percent.
China's exports to Africa, Latin America and North America topped the list, the China Daily said.
Japan, Hong Kong and the United States remained China's largest export markets, the newspaper said, but gave no details.
